newsitem.title: USA: Florida's elderly key to Dole campaign.
newsitem.headline: Florida's elderly key to Dole campaign.

text.p: Bob Dole is trailing in traditionally Republican Florida because voters in the grayest of states are convinced he wants to cut Medicare benefits, political experts and analysts said.

Florida Republican Party Chairman Tom Slade said President Clinton's attack on the Republican Medicare proposals is "probably the largest of the reasons" Clinton holds a five-to 11-point polling lead in Florida, which no Democratic presidential candidate has carried in 20 years.
"We've got to bring the seniors back home," said Slade. "How they think and feel is enormously important in the outcome."

Florida is the nation's oldest state, measured both by the median age of its population and the percentage of the population over 65, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Because the elderly vote in greater numbers than any other age group, 40 percent of Floridians expected to cast ballots in the presidential election are over age 60.

"Bob Dole's record on proposing cuts to Medicare and Medicaid and the uncertainty over where he'll be able to find the money to pay for his tax cut has certainly affected how seniors feel in this race," said Jo Maglino, Florida press secretary for the Clinton-Gore campaign.

Democrats' portrayal of the Republican proposals as Medicare "cuts" infuriates Republicans, who say the difference between the two parties' plans for health insurance reform boils down to $137 per beneficiary per year.

But the detailed charts and technical data needed to make that point make for dull television and would never fit in a 30-second ad, said Slade. Simply calling the president "a bold-faced liar" would alienate voters as well, he said.
"We'll have to do as much direct mail to seniors as we can do about the subject," Slade said. "You're talking about enormous economic resources ...it's an expensive fix."
The Clinton campaign hit hardest on Medicare before Dole was nominated at the Republican convention, when spending limits kept him from launching a counter attack in Florida.

Dole did stress Medicare during his Florida visit last week, his first since winning the Republican nomination. He called the Democrats' tactics "mediscare" and told elderly condominium dwellers that he didn't want to cut Medicare.
But denials are also dicey, said Susan MacManus, a University of South Florida political scientist and expert on gender politics.
"Every time they open it up, it just reminds people of it again," MacManus said.
Persuading the elderly that Dole equals Medicare cuts is part of a Clinton strategy of peeling off enough normally Republican constitutents to carry the state, she said.

Elderly women, who tend to have fewer pension benefits and less economic security than men, are escpecially deserting Dole, MacManus said, while other traditional Republican voters such as business leaders and the Cuban-American community are not making up the difference, political analysts say.
Among Cuban immigrants, party loyalty is wavering this year because of Republican immigration proposals, MacManus said.

"The issue about the schooling for children of immigrants has been a real problem for Republicans and their leaders in south Florida," MacManus said. "I've seen estimates that 15 to 35 percent of Hispanics, Cubans especially, might be voting Clinton this time on that issue alone."
Carrying Florida, with its 25 electoral votes, is crucial, the analysts and party officials agreed.
"If Dole loses Florida, he goes back to Kansas," said Craig.
